---
title: "Population comparisons and sampled variation"
---

The [preceding page](structured-data.qmd) identified participants and items as repeated units before introducing a mixed-model formula. We now distinguish the planned population comparisons from variation across those sampled units.

Suppose an experiment compares two constructions across sampled participants and sentence items. The construction contrast is the quantity of theoretical interest. We want one population coefficient describing the difference between those two conditions.

Participants and items play another role. The observed people represent possible people who could have taken part, and the observed sentences represent possible items that could instantiate the constructions. Mixed-effects terminology distinguishes population-level coefficients, called [**fixed effects**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html), from group-level deviations modeled as draws from a population distribution, called [**random effects**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html).

## Begin with the scientific target

Let $C_i=1$ mark the target construction and $C_i=0$ mark the control. A coefficient $\beta_C$ represents the population comparison between those declared conditions:

$$
\operatorname{E}(Y_i\mid C_i=1)
-\operatorname{E}(Y_i\mid C_i=0)
=\beta_C
$$

for a linear model without other changing predictors.

The labels *target* and *control* are not treated as a random sample from a population of arbitrary condition names. They define the comparison targeted by the hypothesis.

A fixed effect is a coefficient that the model does not itself treat as varying across levels of a grouping factor. In this example, it represents the construction comparison in the population relation. The word *fixed* does not mean that the coefficient is known, constant across every conceivable population, or measured without uncertainty.

## Represent sampled variation

Participants may differ in baseline ratings, and items may differ in baseline acceptability. The analysis usually does not seek 60 unrelated participant coefficients and 40 unrelated item coefficients as its primary result. It seeks population distributions that describe how sampled levels vary.

For participant $j$, write a deviation $b_j$. A random effects model treats

$$
b_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^2).
$$

The standard deviation $\tau$ describes participant to participant variation. Each observed participant receives an estimated deviation under that shared distribution.

The same logic can apply to sentence items. A separate distribution describes how item baselines vary around the population relation. These distributions connect the observed levels to the broader populations identified from the sampling design.

## Do not use storage type as the criterion

Condition, participant, item, and dialect region may all be stored as categorical columns. Their storage type does not determine their modeling role.

Ask instead:

1. Are coefficients for these particular levels the scientific target?
2. Or are the observed levels sampled instances from a population across which the claim should generalize?

Five declared experimental conditions are usually represented by fixed contrasts because those contrasts state the hypothesis. Fifty participant identifiers usually index random effects because the claim is not restricted to those fifty people.

Context can change the answer. A study may compare exactly five dialect regions because their historical differences are the target. That analysis needs fixed contrasts among those regions. Another study may sample many communities to estimate broader regional variation. A group distribution may then match the target better.

## Separate a predictor from a grouping index

Participant age is a measured predictor. Participant identifier is a grouping index. Adding a participant random effect does not replace the age coefficient. The random effect represents remaining participant variation after the modeled predictors have been included.

Likewise, an item's construction condition is a predictor, while item identifier indexes persistent item variation. One row can contain both roles because the roles answer different questions.

This distinction prevents a common mistake: treating every source of variation as an unnamed group deviation. If a measured property encodes a theoretical contrast, place that contrast in the population relation. Let the group distribution represent remaining variation around it.

## State the populations in words

For the construction experiment, a useful target statement is:

> The fixed condition coefficient represents the target minus control comparison. Participant and item effects represent variation across the participant and sentence populations sampled by the design.

This sentence identifies the target comparison and the two generalization populations. Without those statements, the labels *fixed* and *random* provide little information.

The distinction also limits the conclusion. If the study samples many participants but uses one item, a participant random effect cannot create evidence across items. The model can represent only populations for which the design supplies levels.

::: {.callout-note title="Check the target"}
A study compares three writing systems and aims to report those three specific differences. Should writing system identity be random because it is categorical? State the exact comparison before choosing the model term.
:::

The [next page](random-effects.qmd) shows how a shared group distribution produces partial pooling.
